content: Coconut oil, also referred to as coconut butter, is a tropical oil derived from dried coconut meat, known as copra. The term copra originates from the Malayalam word kopra, meaning dried coconut. The Philippines, the largest global exporter of coconut oil, generates approximately 7% of its total export income from this product. The commercial production of coconut oil began in the 1860s, initiated by merchants in the South Seas and South Asia. Physical Properties Coconut oil is composed of approximately 90% saturated fat. It primarily contains medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs), with its fatty acid profile consisting of about 92% saturated fatty acids, 6% monounsaturated fatty acids, and 2% polyunsaturated fatty acids. Among the saturated fatty acids, lauric acid constitutes the largest proportion at 44.6%, followed by myristic acid (16.8%), palmitic acid (8.2%), and caprylic acid (8%). In total, coconut oil contains seven different saturated fatty acids. Its only monounsaturated fatty acid is oleic acid, and its only polyunsaturated fatty acid is linoleic acid. Unrefined coconut oil has a melting point of 24–25°C (76°F) and a smoke point of 170°C (350°F). Refined coconut oil, on the other hand, has a higher smoke point of 232°C (450°F). Due to its high saturated fat content, coconut oil is one of the most stable oils, resistant to oxidation and rancidity, with a shelf life of up to two years. To maximize its shelf life, it is best stored in solid form, below 24.5°C. Health Effects Heart Disease The consumption of saturated fats has been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Given its high saturated fat content, regular consumption of coconut oil may elevate this risk. However, a 2004 study published in Clinical Biochemistry found that virgin coconut oil reduced LDL cholesterol (associated with cardiovascular disease) while increasing beneficial HDL cholesterol levels. An epidemiological study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition examined two indigenous populations whose diets derived 63% and 34% of their energy from coconuts, respectively, and found no increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Another 2004 article in the same journal suggested that the link between saturated fats and heart disease might be a statistical error. Additionally, some studies have indicated that coconut oil may aid in weight loss and recovery from poisoning. Antimicrobial Effects Research conducted at University College Hospital in Ibadan, Nigeria, and published in the Journal of Medicinal Food demonstrated that coconut oil is effective against certain strains of Candida, the fungus responsible for candidiasis in humans. The study's authors recommended coconut oil as a treatment for fungal infections. Types of Coconut Oil Virgin Coconut Oil Virgin coconut oil is extracted from fresh coconuts rather than dried copra. It is typically produced using one of three methods: 1. Quick Drying: Fresh coconut meat is quickly dried and then pressed to extract the oil. 2. Wet-Milling (Coconut Milk): Oil is extracted from fresh coconut meat without prior drying. Coconut milk is first expressed by pressing, and the oil is then separated from the water using methods such as boiling, fermentation, refrigeration, enzymatic processes, or mechanical centrifugation. 3. Wet-Milling (Direct Micro Expelling): The water content of fresh coconut meat is adjusted, and the flesh is pressed to directly extract free-flowing oil. Unlike olive oil, there is no global standard or governing body to define or classify coconut oil as virgin. However, the Philippines has established a governmental standard through its Department of Science and Technology (DOST). Refined Coconut Oil Refined coconut oil, often referred to as RBD (refined, bleached, and deodorized) coconut oil, is derived from copra. Copra is dried coconut meat, which can be processed through smoke drying, sun drying, or kiln drying. The crude coconut oil extracted from copra is not suitable for consumption and must undergo refining. Hydrogenated Coconut Oil Coconut oil is sometimes partially or fully hydrogenated to increase its melting point in warmer climates. This process increases the saturated fat content and may produce trans fats. Fractionated Coconut Oil Fractionated coconut oil is a processed form in which most long-chain triglycerides are removed, leaving primarily medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs), such as caprylic and capric acids. This oil, also known as caprylic/capric triglyceride or MCT oil, is fully saturated, making it highly heat-stable with an almost indefinite shelf life. Applications Cooking Coconut oil is widely used in cooking, particularly for frying. In regions where coconut oil is a staple, refined oil is the most commonly used form. It is also a popular ingredient in South Asian curries, adding flavor and richness. Manufacturing Coconut oil is used in large quantities for the production of margarine, soap, and cosmetics. Hydrogenated or partially hydrogenated coconut oil is a common ingredient in non-dairy creamers and snack foods. Fractionated coconut oil is utilized in the production of essences, massage oils, and cosmetics. Additionally, coconut oil serves as a key component in industrial lubricants, such as those used in the cold rolling of steel strips. Cosmetics and Skin Treatments Coconut oil is an effective skin moisturizer and softener. Studies have shown that extra virgin coconut oil is as safe and effective as mineral oil for moisturizing, with no reported adverse reactions. While unsuitable for use with latex condoms, coconut oil is an inexpensive lubricant for sexual intercourse, though it may cause allergic reactions in some individuals. In India and Sri Lanka, coconut oil is commonly used for hair styling and to cool or soothe the scalp. In Tamil Nadu and other coastal regions of India, people often apply coconut oil to their skin and hair before bathing in warm water to maintain health and hydration. As a Fuel Traditional Use Coconut oil has been traditionally used as fuel in oil lamps. Diesel Engines Coconut oil has been tested as a biodiesel feedstock for diesel engines, including power generators and transportation. It can be blended to produce biodiesel or used directly in unmodified engines under certain conditions. However, its higher viscosity (up to 10 times that of diesel) and solidification point (22–25°C) require modifications, such as fuel tank heaters, in temperate climates. Coconut oil has been used as a fuel source in remote communities with abundant coconut supplies and milling capacity. During the Bougainville conflict in the 1990s, islanders used coconut oil to fuel vehicles when cut off from conventional fuel supplies. Aircraft Fuel In February 2008, a biofuel trial sponsored by Virgin Atlantic used a mixture of coconut oil and babassu oil to partially power one engine of a Boeing 747. Philippines In January 2008, a company in the Philippines converted coconut oil into engine oil using Korean biotechnology. The resulting product, S-9 lubricating motor oil, was tested in over 400 vehicles and demonstrated benefits such as reduced fuel consumption (up to 45%), decreased smoke emissions (up to 95%), increased power, and cooler engine operating temperatures. The company produces 5,000 liters of this motor oil per month.
